title: Stage A — Story Identity
label: Story identity
intro: Begin with the spark. We’ll shape what makes this story yours before building its architecture.
purpose: Find the story’s distinctive dramatic and personal center.
why: Later decisions become easier to test against a clear identity.
method: Start with raw material; then form a working story statement and compare intended meaning with likely reader experience.
exercise: Write three one-sentence versions: the image that started it, the event that drives it, and why you want to tell it.
criteria: The identity gives both readers a reason to care and you a test for what belongs.
watch_for: A premise that describes only its setting or events, or a theme stated as a lesson before the story has tested it.
output: Creative identity and foundational story statement.
completion: You can name the spark, dramatic interest, and personal reason to write without settling every plot detail.
sources: Lisa Cron (Story Genius): start from what the story is really about—the protagonist’s inner struggle and the point it makes—rather than from plot events. Jessica Brody (Save the Cat! Writes a Novel): test the idea as a one-sentence pitch with a flawed hero, a catalyst, and a goal. Planner synthesis: keep the original spark visible and compare your intent with the likely reader experience.

title: Stage B — Reader Promise
label: Reader promise
intro: Consider the experience the story offers—not only what happens, but what a reader comes for.
purpose: Clarify audience, genre expectations, scale, and the emotional and intellectual promise.
why: This helps keep the opening, middle, and ending feeling like parts of the same book.
method: Compare your intended experience with genre signals and likely reader expectations; decide which conventions to honor, bend, or subvert.
exercise: Complete: 'Readers who enjoy ___ can expect ___, while this novel makes that experience distinctive by ___.'.
criteria: The promise guides the opening and ending while leaving room for originality.
watch_for: Treating genre as a rigid formula or ignoring expectations the book itself creates.
output: Reader, genre, scope, and narrative-promise specification.
completion: You can describe the likely reader, the experience promised, and the trade-offs you intend.
sources: Jessica Brody (Save the Cat! Writes a Novel): her ten story genres (such as Whydunit, Rites of Passage, and Dude with a Problem) describe the kind of story a reader is promised, independent of bookstore category. Planner synthesis: decide which conventions to honor, bend, or subvert, and name the trade-offs.

title: Stage C — Tone, Voice & Style
label: Tone, voice & style
intro: Translate the intended experience into choices about atmosphere, viewpoint, voice, and prose.
purpose: Create a usable style and tone charter rather than a loose list of adjectives.
why: These choices control intimacy, information, emotional range, and the prose texture readers experience.
method: Work from broad tone to atmosphere, narrator and viewpoint, then prose habits and guardrails. Treat sample prose as a demonstration, not a rule.
exercise: Draft a neutral moment twice: once in your intended voice and once in a voice you reject. Compare rhythm, detail, distance, and effect.
criteria: The charter explains what to do, what to watch for, and when tonal contrast is intentional.
watch_for: Adjectives without observable prose choices, or rigid prohibitions that flatten the writing.
output: Style and Tone Charter, including viewpoint rules and optional original samples.
completion: You can make consistent choices about narration, viewpoint, prose, and tonal shifts.
sources: Lisa Cron (Story Genius): readers experience events through the protagonist’s subjective view—what things mean to them—so viewpoint and voice carry the story’s meaning. Planner synthesis: the source books concentrate on story and structure; the Style and Tone Charter turns tonal adjectives into observable prose choices.

title: Stage D — Theme
label: Theme
intro: Let the novel explore its ideas through conflict and consequence instead of explaining what readers should think.
purpose: Connect story questions to competing values, choices, and outcomes.
why: A live thematic tension gives events depth without turning characters into mouthpieces.
method: Phrase themes as questions, give credible characters different answers, and trace choices that test those answers.
exercise: Write two opposing answers to a central question; give each a persuasive advocate and a meaningful cost.
criteria: The theme is dramatized through decisions and consequences; the conclusion need not dictate one interpretation.
watch_for: Confusing the author’s belief with every character’s belief or stating a theme without putting it under pressure.
output: Thematic framework linked to character, conflict, and ending.
completion: You can identify the central question and see how the story will test it.
sources: Jessica Brody (Save the Cat! Writes a Novel): theme is what the hero needs to learn, often hinted early (Theme Stated) and explored through the B Story. Lisa Cron (Story Genius): meaning grows from the protagonist’s struggle with a mistaken belief. Planner synthesis: phrase the theme as a live question with credible opposing answers.

title: Stage E — Characters
label: Characters
intro: Build only as much character detail as the story needs to make choices and relationships convincing.
purpose: Establish a functional cast with agency, motives, resistance, relationships, and possible change.
why: Character logic powers plot; intentional limits keep dossiers useful rather than encyclopedic.
method: For principal characters, connect goals, motivation, beliefs, strengths, limits, history, relationships, and choices. For secondary characters, begin with function.
exercise: Choose a pressure point: what does the character do, why does it make sense to them, what does it cost, and how does someone respond?
criteria: Motives explain decisions, choices have consequences, the protagonist acts, and important characters have distinct functions and voices.
watch_for: Biography without story relevance, an antagonist who only obstructs, or change unsupported by events.
output: Principal character dossiers, relationship/conflict map, and character-arc plans.
completion: The central choices can be traced to character motives, and the cast has a reason to be present.
sources: Lisa Cron (Story Genius): know the protagonist’s desire, the misbelief in its way, and where that misbelief came from before plotting. Jessica Brody (Save the Cat! Writes a Novel): a hero has flaws, a want, and a deeper need. Planner synthesis: develop secondary characters by function first, and test the cast for agency and redundancy.

title: Stage F — World & Internal Logic
label: World & logic
intro: Develop the parts of the world that shape action, then decide what readers need to learn and when.
purpose: Create a relevant world reference and dependable internal rules.
why: Material, social, historical, and speculative constraints affect what characters can plausibly do.
method: For each world element, ask how it affects behavior, conflict, atmosphere, or theme; separate author knowledge from reader-facing information.
exercise: Follow one important rule into daily life, power, available resources, and a plot choice.
criteria: Story-critical rules are consistent and their consequences are understood; exposition is intentionally paced.
watch_for: Encyclopedic detail with no story function, or a convenient exception that bypasses an established constraint.
output: Story-relevant world reference, reveal plan, and internal consistency rules.
completion: The world permits the plot, constrains it meaningfully, and has no rule gap that breaks a core event.
sources: Planner synthesis: the source books treat setting mainly as pressure on character and plot, so this stage develops only the parts of the world that change behavior, conflict, atmosphere, or theme, and keeps author knowledge separate from reader knowledge.

title: Stage G — Conflict & Plot
label: Conflict & plot
intro: Turn character pressure into consequential events, escalating choices, and earned outcomes.
purpose: Design a plot architecture whose events cause, complicate, and pay off one another.
why: Causality makes momentum and a climax feel earned without imposing a formula.
method: Define goal, resistance, stakes, and dramatic question; sketch turns; then test each link with because/therefore and the opposition’s response.
exercise: Write a five-link causal chain from the opening disruption to a decisive climax. Circle any link that needs out-of-character behavior.
criteria: The protagonist has a reason to act, opposition adapts, stakes escalate, and the climax grows from prior decisions.
watch_for: Coincidence replacing choice, consequences that disappear, or a resolution unrelated to the central conflict.
output: Macro plot outline and causal structure.
completion: The main story can be summarized as motivated actions and consequential reactions.
sources: K.M. Weiland (Structuring Your Novel and its Workbook): structural turning points—inciting event, plot points, pinch points, midpoint, climax—with the protagonist reacting until the midpoint and acting after it. Jessica Brody (Save the Cat! Writes a Novel): the fifteen-beat sheet, from the Catalyst and Break into 2 through All Is Lost to the Finale. Lisa Cron (Story Genius): plot as a cause-and-effect chain driven by the protagonist’s inner struggle. Where they differ: Weiland and Brody begin from structural beats, while Cron builds outward from the protagonist’s internal change; this stage uses beats as checkpoints and causality as the test.

title: Stage H — Subplots & Integration
label: Subplots
intro: Connect secondary threads to the same novel so they deepen, complicate, or echo the central story.
purpose: Make subplots and relationships function as part of one narrative system.
why: Integration protects focus and lets supporting threads affect how the main story unfolds.
method: For each thread, identify purpose, conflict, progression, thematic value, intersections, and resolution; consider removal or repositioning.
exercise: Temporarily remove a subplot. Name the plot, character, and thematic loss; if there is none, reconsider its role.
criteria: Each substantial thread has a distinct purpose and meaningful interaction with the main plot.
watch_for: Subplots that repeat the main plot without changing it or accumulate because an idea is appealing.
completion: Every major thread has a function and clear connection, or an intentional reason to remain separate.
sources: Jessica Brody (Save the Cat! Writes a Novel): the B Story—often a relationship—carries the theme and helps the hero learn it. Planner synthesis: test each thread by imagining the novel without it.

title: Stage I — Scenes & Chapters
label: Scenes & chapters
intro: Move from broad plot to scenes that change something—without outlining the manuscript sentence by sentence.
purpose: Create a flexible sequence and a purposeful opening-chapter specification.
why: Scene objectives, resistance, change, and information flow translate architecture into draftable work.
method: Outline major sequences, then key scenes with objective, resistance, turn, consequence, information, and emotional movement.
exercise: For the opening, write one line each for what readers know, feel, question, and anticipate at the end of Chapter One.
criteria: The opening embodies the novel’s promise, and planned scenes create progression without requiring every minor beat.
watch_for: Planning every sentence, scenes with no change, or opening exposition that delays the story’s invitation.
output: Preliminary sequence/scene/chapter map and opening requirements.
completion: You know the opening’s job and next meaningful story movement, while leaving room for discovery.
sources: K.M. Weiland (Structuring Your Novel), building on Dwight V. Swain: scenes of goal, conflict, and disaster, followed by sequels of reaction, dilemma, and decision. Lisa Cron (Story Genius): plan scenes as cards that record the event, what the protagonist realizes, and how it causes the next scene. Jessica Brody (Save the Cat! Writes a Novel): the Opening Image and Setup show the hero’s world and flaws before the Catalyst.

title: Stage J — Continuity & Readiness
label: Continuity & readiness
intro: Set up a light continuity system, record intentional unknowns, and decide what is ready to discover by drafting.
purpose: Keep the manuscript coherent and make a realistic Chapter One readiness judgment.
why: Readiness separates genuine structural risks from harmless open questions.
method: Record likely continuity facts; track setups, reveals, viewpoint, and style constraints; assess unknowns by drafting risk.
exercise: Sort open questions into: answer before drafting, monitor while drafting, and discover through drafting. Say why.
criteria: Essential foundations support the opening; remaining uncertainty is named and bounded.
watch_for: A superficial green checklist, or treating every blank as a blocker.
output: Continuity ledger, tailored quality checklist, unresolved decisions, and Ready to Write Chapter One? assessment.
completion: You can name what is ready, what risk needs attention, and what Chapter One should test.
sources: Planner synthesis of the Cookbook’s continuity and revision standards: track setups and payoffs, information flow, and viewpoint rules in a light ledger, and judge readiness by risk rather than completeness—without demanding perfection before drafting.
